articles.title: A magnitude 7.1 earthquake shakes part of southern Japan but no tsunami detected
articles.description: Reporters watch the news showing a large quake and possible one meter tsunami wave in Southern Japan, from an office in Tokyo on July 28, 2026. A strong 7.1-magnitude earthquake hit southern Japan, the Japan Meteorological Agency said, issuing a tsunami alert. The tremor also measured at the highest possible level seven on Japan’s own Shindo scale of shaking, the agency said. (Photo by Andrew CABALLERO-REYNOLDS / AFP via Getty Images)

articles.title: Antigua and Barbuda: 5 ways the Red Cross is institutionalizing anticipatory action in the Americas in 2026
articles.description: Countries: Antigua and Barbuda, Barbados, Belize, Bolivia (Plurinational State of), Chile, Colombia, Cuba, Dominica, Dominican Republic, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Haiti, Mexico, Panama, Paraguay, Saint Kitts and Nevis, Uruguay In Latin America and the Caribbean, anticipatory action – which uses forecasts to act before a hazard hits communities - has moved from a new concept to a daily practice that saves lives before an emergency strikes. Throughout 2026, the Red Cross network in the Americas promoted regulatory frameworks, signed alliances with scientific organizations, and activated protocols on the ground so families are safer and better prepared for crises. Here are five ways the Red Cross is institutionalizing anticipatory action in the Americas in 2026: 1. Governance, laws, and national roadmaps In 2026, Ecuador approved its National Guide for Anticipatory Actions after regulating its Organic Law on Disaster Risk Management. In November, the Ecuadorian Red Cross, working with the IFRC, the National Institute of Meteorology and Hydrology (INAMHI), and the National Secretariat for Risk Management under the Kawsay project, University IKIAM, and others, drafted its Amazonian Simplified Early Action Protocol (S EAP) for pluvial floods in Napo, Orellana, Pastaza, and Sucumbíos. The team defined selection criteria, an initial budget, and concrete measures to protect health, water access, shelter, income, and livelihoods for Amazonian families. On November 18, 2026, the Bolivian Red Cross launched the Humanidad que Anticipa (Humanity That Anticipates) initiative, backed by the Spanish Agency for International Development Cooperation (AECID), the Italian Red Cross, the Swiss Red Cross, and the IFRC. The event brought together 80 participants from nearly 30 institutions and closed with cooperation agreements with the Vice Ministry of Civil Defense and Save the Children to coordinate actions that protect the most vulnerable populations in the Amazon. "In Bolivia, we are institutionalizing new ways of managing disaster risk that focus on people and community well-being. We designed the Humanity That Anticipates initiative to unite the efforts of the Red Cross Movement, international cooperation, and the State, including Civil Defense and the National Service of Hydrology and Meteorology, laying the groundwork for sustained work in communities and local governments," said Edgar Butrón Ledezma, Executive Director of the Bolivian Red Cross. On 18 November, the Bolivian Red Cross launched Humanidad que Anticipa (Humanity That Anticipates) to institutionalize anticipatory action in Bolivia, strengthen local capacities, and protect vulnerable communities before disasters strike. 2. Scientific alliances for better action In 2026, National Societies strengthened coordination with meteorological institutes to turn climate data into early warnings and timely aid for people. In the Eastern Caribbean, Red Cross National Societies in Antigua and Barbuda, Dominica, and Saint Kitts and Nevis harmonized scientific data and triggers for their simplified protocols against tropical storms. The Haitian Red Cross leads a similar process for tropical cyclones. In South America, the Uruguayan Red Cross strengthened its technical collaboration with the national meteorological service. Teams presented their drought assessment and coordinated early actions for the drought Early Action Protocol (EAP) currently under development. In Central America and the Spanish-speaking Caribbean, these partnerships delivered direct results. The Panamanian Red Cross signed a Memorandum of Understanding with the Institute of Meteorology and Hydrology of Panama (IMHPA) to support its simplified protocols against floods and dengue. "Anticipatory action allows us to mitigate early the effects of any disease, outbreak, or adverse natural event. Right now, we are working on two projects, one for dengue and one for floods, so we can start acting and responding before the impact affects communities," explained Henry Staples, health focal point of the Panamanian Red Cross. Meanwhile, the Cuban Red Cross applied lessons from the activation funded by the Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF) ahead of Hurricane Melissa, where it moved key supplies closer to communities days before landfall, and designed its intense rainfall protocol alongside the country's scientific institutions. "Since 2025, Cuba activated its country-level anticipatory action framework, and with prepositioned resources we delivered the first response. This process has also allowed us to build capacities, conduct training, and create an Early Action Protocol in Cuba by meeting with the scientific entities providing data through the Institute of Meteorology, the National Institute of Hydraulic Resources, and Civil Defense to preposition resources before another event occurs," noted Dr. Carlos Ricardo Pérez Díaz, Executive President of the Cuban Red Cross. 3. Pilots and community validation For a protocol to work, it must reflect the reality of people living in at-risk areas. That is why 2026 focused on field simulations and participatory design alongside local communities. Barbados and Belize Red Cross teams carried out simulations and engaged more than 50 national and regional actors to validate triggers and early actions for their first tropical cyclone protocols. In the Dominican Republic, the Red Cross drove the national technical group while advancing its heavy rainfall protocol. In 2026, the Paraguayan Red Cross simulated the delivery of cash transfers under its drought Simplified Early Action Protocol, designed so families receive financial support three months in advance to protect their livelihoods. The team also took part in the National Emergency Executive Councilto coordinate preventive measures ahead of El Niño. This effort builds on six community action plans and a pilot early warning system in Asunción. 4. Public health and private sector partnerships Anticipatory action in the Americas also expanded to prevent epidemic outbreaks and brought in new partners that strengthen local response capacity. The Guatemalan Red Cross worked with medical specialists to design its Dengue Early Action Protocol and identify indicators to curb infections before an outbreak, including developing a nationally harmonized trigger for dengue anticipatory action. In Mexico, the Red Cross coordinated community brigades and local governments to protect health, lives, and family livelihoods. It is also promoting a model where the private sector joins as a technical and operational partner beyond financial contributions. "Anticipatory action is an opportunity to preposition resources and reduce the impacts of natural hazards at the community level, in health as well as in protecting livelihoods and life itself. We want other sectors, including the private sector, to join not only financially, but also with technical capacities, information, and volunteering, standing with us as true allies," said Gabriel Reyes, Operational Lead for the Climate Resilience project at the Mexican Red Cross. A Mexican Red Cross volunteer helps a community member in Veracruz to develop his Family Emergency Plan. 5. Activations that protect lives before disaster strikes During 2026, four countries activated Early Action Protocols (EAPs) in the region and delivered assistance before hazards hit: Colombia: After holding its first National Risk Management Platform and declaring 2026 the "Year of Anticipatory Action in Colombia," the Colombian Red Cross activated its simplified drought protocol in June at the earliest signs of drought. Backed by the IFRC Disaster Response Emergency Fund (IFRC-DREF), the operation provided anticipatory assistance to 4,765 people across five municipalities in Cesar and Tolima between June and September. Chile: Ratified within the National Strategy to Strengthen Wildfire Management 2026-2027 alongside SENAPRED and CONAF, the Chilean Red Cross activated the world's first Wildfire Simplified Early Action Protocol. Actions included issuing early warnings and distributing evacuation kits and firebreak tools so rural families could protect their homes and evacuate in time. El Salvador: Supported by its National Action Plan and Early Warning System, the Salvadoran Red Cross activated its full drought protocol to safeguard family livelihoods and food security before peak water scarcity hit. Guatemala: Following forecasts from the National Institute of Seismology, Volcanology, Meteorology and Hydrology (INSIVUMEH) regarding rainfall deficits and El Niño conditions, the Guatemalan Red Cross activated its Drought Early Action Protocol in June to provide anticipatory assistance to 10,000 people across prioritized municipalities in the Dry Corridor and other vulnerable areas. With support from the IFRC-DREF, local Red Cross teams implemented multipurpose cash transfers and water, sanitation, and hygiene interventions to protect the food security and livelihoods of high-risk households. As part of the anticipatory actions under the Early Action Protocol for drought, the Colombian Red Cross distributed 100 kits for the treatment and storage of safe water to families in the village of El Carmen, in the municipality of El Paso, Cesar. The results of 2026 confirm that the region is shifting toward a more preventive, people-centered approach to risk management. With active protocols, stronger scientific data, and community leadership, National Red Cross Societies are helping thousands of families across Latin America and the Caribbean face climate threats with greater protection and well-being.

articles.title: Classes halted in parts of Iloilo after 5.1 magnitude Antique quake
articles.description: ILOILO CITY — A magnitude 5.1 earthquake that struck Antique on Wednesday morning prompted the suspension of classes in several Iloilo municipalities and the evacuation of students, government employees, and people transacting in public offices. Authorities ordered the evacuation as they began inspections of buildings for possible structural damage. Based on the Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology (Phivolcs)’ initial bulletin, the earthquake occurred at 7:29 a.m., with its epicenter located 14 kilometers southeast of Valderrama, Antique, at a depth of 10 kilometers. The earthquake was felt across Western Visayas and parts of the Negros Island Region, Central Visayas, and Romblon. […]... articles.title: 'Secret emergency' doomsday rumors send Trump officials scrambling
articles.description: Stock up on food and medicine. Fill containers with water. Prepare to live off the grid for at least 90 days. Those were among the warnings circulating on social media in recent weeks, as online posts predicted a looming national catastrophe and urged Americans to prepare for the worst. The supposed warning signs? A nationwide flight shutdown, disruptions to banking and technology services and a routine federal emergency alert test — seemingly unrelated events that some online users portrayed as evidence of a coordinated cyberattack or impending emergency. The doomsday predictions lack credible evidence. But the speculation comes as the nation’s aging infrastructure faces mounting vulnerabilities from extreme weather, rising energy demands and cyberthreats — raising legitimate questions about the country’s preparedness for major disruptions. Federal officials have said they found no evidence that the latest disruptions were connected or that a nationwide emergency was imminent. And some emergency management experts warn that false alarms can undermine public trust in official warnings and complicate disaster response when real emergencies strike. Still, the attention surrounding these unfounded predictions does not necessarily mean they have gained widespread acceptance. Joseph Uscinski, a political science professor at the University of Miami who studies conspiracy theories, cautioned against interpreting viral posts as evidence of a broader shift in public beliefs. “Your average conspiracy theory dies on the vine,” he said, noting that many fade as the news cycle moves on. Uscinski described the reaction as a recurring pattern: A major event sparks conspiracy theories, those claims attract attention and then eventually fade, only for the cycle to repeat when another event captures the public’s attention. Some of the latest rumors appeared to gain traction ahead of Tuesday’s nationwide Emergency Alert System test, which interrupted television and radio broadcasts across the country. The Federal Emergency Management Agency, or FEMA, and the Federal Communications Commission, or FCC, had announced the Nov. 17 test in September as part of routine efforts to evaluate the nation’s emergency warning infrastructure. Federal rules require nationwide testing at least once every three years. The timing of the test, combined with recent outages and national security concerns, fueled speculation that the government was preparing Americans for a major catastrophe. FEMA addressed the claims on Facebook, saying the test was scheduled in advance and unrelated to any impending disaster. “We love a good fan theory as much as anyone, but there is no secret emergency happening here,” the agency’s post read. From technical glitches to doomsday warnings The online speculation followed several high-profile disruptions this month, including a major Microsoft service outage Nov. 12-14, and a nationwide ground stop issued by the Federal Aviation Administration on Nov. 13. Microsoft attributed its disruptions to technical problems. And the FAA blamed work by a contractor upgrading a router in Arkansas. But this week brought more disruptions: to several major banks Monday, to Apple services and the National Security Agency’s internal network Tuesday. Those also were separate technical issues, officials said. Adding to the national security concerns, CNN reported Monday that U.S. intelligence suggested Iran was developing plans to potentially target senior Trump administration officials with a radioactive “dirty bomb” or chemical weapon in Washington, D.C. US Senate panel grills Trump cyber director about outages making people ‘jittery’ U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Tuesday that he did not believe there was an imminent threat to Washington. Iran also denied the allegations. During a congressional hearing Wednesday, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told lawmakers that threats from Iran against Americans at home and abroad had increased substantially. Asked specifically about the reported dirty-bomb plot, Clayton declined to discuss the intelligence but acknowledged that threats involving weapons capable of causing mass casualties were not new. Despite those explanations, social media posts increasingly portrayed the events as connected. Some TikTok videos warned of a 90-day nationwide blackout that was to begin Nov. 17, while other videos encouraged viewers to stockpile emergency supplies, including water, food and medicine. One widely circulated video manipulated footage of President Donald Trump speaking at a Nov. 9 news conference to make it appear that he had announced an impending blackout, according to a PolitiFact investigation. Trump made no such announcement. The account sharing the manipulated footage also promoted cryptocurrency purchases ahead of the supposed national emergency. Other online posts pointed to a federal Department of Defense initiative announced in September to help military installations operate independently of civilian power grids for at least 90 days. The initiative, known as FORTRESS America, is intended to strengthen military readiness during potential disruptions. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin also dismissed the online warnings, telling Fox News that Americans did not need to stockpile supplies in anticipation of widespread disruptions to electricity or to food and water sources. Vice President JD Vance similarly sought to ease concerns Monday, saying Americans did not need to build bunkers or rush to stockpile food and water in response to the recent outages. “We do not see some crisis coming down, but you have to be prepared for everything,” Vance said during an interview with Fox News. Other countries, including the United Kingdom, France and Germany, have urged residents to prepare for severe weather, cyberattacks and other emergencies –– adding to confusion among some Americans about whether they should take similar precautions. The UK launched its “Be Ready” campaign in October suggesting a three-day supply in case of emergency. Real vulnerabilities The conspiracy theories have emerged against a backdrop of genuine concerns about the nation’s aging infrastructure and growing cybersecurity threats, which have exposed vulnerabilities in systems Americans rely on for electricity, transportation, healthcare and emergency services. The American Society of Civil Engineers gave U.S. infrastructure an overall C grade in its 2025 report card, a slight improvement from the C- awarded in 2021. The national report card is released every four years. FEMA chief, US House members push for emergency management changes But the organization warned that significant vulnerabilities remain. The nation’s energy and aviation infrastructure each received a D+, and the report estimated a $3.7 trillion gap between planned infrastructure investments and what is needed to bring the country’s systems into good working order. The recent disruptions also drew scrutiny on Capitol Hill on Thursday, where lawmakers questioned Trump’s nominee to lead the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, or CISA, about the nation’s ability to withstand cyberthreats. “American citizens are jittery,” Michigan Democratic U.S. Sen. Elissa Slotkin said during the Senate Homeland Security Committee hearing, raising concerns about the Trump administration’s elimination of more than 1,000 positions at the agency. The nominee, Michael LoSapio, declined to assess the agency’s current resources but said he would evaluate potential gaps and request additional funding if necessary. Cyberattacks are a growing concern for critical infrastructure operators, as hackers target hospitals, utilities, government agencies and other essential services. “Modern society is effectively built on interdependence and high levels of complexity of technologies supporting human systems, and so when you get kind of a localized failure, it can very quickly cascade to more strategic problems,” said Charles Harry, an associate research professor at the University of Maryland who specializes in cybersecurity risk and previously worked for the National Security Agency. Harry pointed to healthcare and transportation as examples of sectors where interconnected systems can allow disruptions to spread far beyond their original source. Hundreds of thousands of cyberattacks occur every day, but most attract little public attention because they cause minimal disruption, Harry said. The landscape is evolving as artificial intelligence gives cybercriminals, state-sponsored hackers and even less sophisticated attackers new tools, putting additional pressure on organizations to address security weaknesses before they can be exploited. “Over the last 12 months, we’ve seen just an explosion in this type of activity, and it means that we’re going to have more frequent attacks, more consequential attacks,” Harry said. When misinformation becomes a public safety threat Beyond the latest doomsday predictions, the spread of false information presents a broader challenge for state and local emergency management agencies, which rely on public trust to communicate accurate information during disasters. FEMA chief decries rumors, disinformation about hurricane recovery as worst ever During an actual emergency, false or misleading information can divert critical resources, delay response efforts and create confusion about evacuation routes, available shelters and government assistance. “Sometimes (misinformation) can even mask itself as being something that comes from us, so you really have to dig deep, look at where the messages are coming from,” said Marc Pappas, the president of the National Emergency Management Association and director of the Rhode Island Emergency Management Agency. The consequences have already played out during real emergencies. Following Hurricanes Helene and Milton in 2024, conspiracy theories shared online alleged that the federal government had deliberately created or steered the storms toward certain communities. Other false claims accused federal officials of withholding disaster assistance, confiscating property and preventing private organizations from delivering supplies. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, or NOAA, publicly debunked the weather manipulation claims, emphasizing that no technology exists to create or steer hurricanes. FEMA also launched an online “rumor response” page to counter misinformation and reassure survivors that assistance remained available. The challenges facing emergency officials come as the Trump administration considers shifting more disaster response responsibilities to state and local governments. During a U.S. House hearing Thursday, FEMA Administrator Cameron Hamilton called for significant changes to the agency, arguing that stronger states would make the nation more prepared and resilient. Some lawmakers questioned whether states have the resources to take on additional responsibilities. “Emergency management is ready. We continue to be ready and prepared for emergencies, threats that happen to occur across the nation,” Pappas told Stateline, arguing that state agencies are well equipped to take on additional disaster response responsibilities.
